2026-03-20

## Loading required package: ggplot2

df <- read.csv("/Users/sarahcampos/Downloads/student_mental_health_burnout_1M.csv")

df$AtRisk <- ifelse(df$risk_level == "High", 1, 0)
df$AtRisk <- as.factor(df$AtRisk)

set.seed(123)
df_sample <- df[sample(nrow(df), 5000), ]

Introduction

Students are increasingly exposed to academic pressure; this poses significant consequences for their mental health. As academic expectations rise, many students experience stress, anxiety and burnout. In turn, this makes it important to identify those who may be at risk. Early identification of vulnerable individuals can support timely interventions and improve overall well-being.(APA) This study examines whether student lifestyle and academic factors can be used to predict mental health risk. Specifically, it seeks to determine whether observable behaviors and academic conditions are sufficient to identify students at risk, or whether psychological indicators provide additional predictive value. By applying classification models, this analysis aims to contribute to a better understanding of how different factors relate to student mental health outcomes.

Problem Definition and Task

This study is framed as a binary classification problem with the objective to predict whether a student is at risk of poor mental health. The input consists of a set of student-level variables such as lifestyle behaviors, academic conditions, and psychological indicators, while the output is a binary variable representing mental health risk status. A prediction is considered correct if the model accurately classifies a student as either at risk (1) or not at risk (0). This problem presents several challenges, including a high degree of class imbalance, as relatively few students fall into the at-risk category, as well as complex relationships between predictors. Additionally, some variables, particularly psychological measures, are closely related to the outcome itself, making it necessary to carefully interpret their role in the models.

Model Definition

Three classification approaches are used in this analysis. Logistic regression serves as a baseline model due to its interpretability and its ability to estimate the probability that a student is at risk. This model assumes a linear relationship between the predictors and the log-odds of the outcome. A decision tree model is also employed to capture potential non-linear relationships and interactions between variables by recursively partitioning the data. Finally, a random forest model is implemented as an ensemble method that combines multiple decision trees to improve predictive performance and reduce overfitting. This approach is particularly useful for capturing complex patterns in large datasets.

Methodology

The variables included in the analysis were selected based on their expected relevance to student mental health. “The dataset contains approximately 1,000,000 observations and includes variables related to stress, anxiety, sleep, and academic performance.” (Kaggle) Two modeling approaches were developed to allow for comparison. The first model focuses on behavioral and academic factors including sleep hours, study hours, screen time, physical activity and financial stress. These variables represent observable characteristics that may provide early signals of mental health risk. The second model expands on this by including additional variables such as exam pressure, academic performance, stress level, anxiety score, depression score and family expectations. These variables capture psychological and contextual factors that are more directly related to mental health outcomes. All continuous variables were inspected for distributional patterns prior to modeling to ensure appropriate interpretation of results.

The primary hypothesis tested in this study is that higher academic workload, measured through study hours and exam pressure, increases the probability that a student is at risk of poor mental health. The dataset used for this analysis contains approximately one million observations, providing a large sample for model training and evaluation. The target variable was constructed from a categorical risk measure and converted into a binary indicator.

To evaluate model performance, the dataset was split into training and testing subsets using a 70/30 split. A 70/30 split is commonly used because it balances the need for sufficient training data with a large enough test set for reliable evaluation.(Gunkurnia) In addition, five-fold cross-validation was applied during model training to improve robustness and reduce overfitting. Since the dataset exhibits severe class imbalance, resampling techniques were applied to ensure that the minority class was adequately represented during training.

Model performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, confusion matrices and balanced accuracy. Balanced accuracy is reported as a proportion between 0 and 1 and can be interpreted as a percentage. It is particularly useful in imbalanced datasets because it accounts for performance across both classes equally. Given the imbalance in the data, particular emphasis was placed on recall and balanced accuracy, as these metrics better reflect the model’s ability to identify at-risk students.

Comparisons between at-risk and non-risk students show consistent directional differences across all variables . At-risk students tend to sleep less and study more, although these differences show substantial overlap, suggesting limited standalone predictive power. In contrast, stress, anxiety, and depression exhibit clear separation between groups, indicating strong discriminative ability. However, this separation also raises concerns about potential overlap with the outcome variable itself, as these measures closely reflect mental health status rather than acting as independent predictors.

Relationships Between Variables

Heat Map of Variables

library(corrplot)

corrplot(cor(df[, sapply(df, is.numeric)], use = "complete.obs"),
         method = "color",
         type = "upper")

The correlation analysis reveals strong relationships among stress, anxiety and depression. This indicates the presence of multicollinearity . This suggests that these variables may represent a shared underlying construct of psychological distress rather than independent factors. As a result, including all three variables may introduce redundancy into the model without substantially improving predictive performance. These findings provide the foundation for the classification models by highlighting which variables are most likely to contribute to predictive performance

Classification Modeling

Create full dataset for modeling

df_full <- df[, c("AtRisk",
                  "sleep_hours",
                  "study_hours_per_day",
                  "screen_time",
                  "physical_activity",
                  "financial_stress",
                  "exam_pressure",
                  "academic_performance",
                  "stress_level",
                  "anxiety_score",
                  "depression_score",
                  "family_expectation")]

Train/test split

set.seed(123)

trainIndex <- createDataPartition(df_full$AtRisk, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)

train_full <- df_full[trainIndex, ]
test_full  <- df_full[-trainIndex, ]

Plot variable importance from random forest

library(caret)

ctrl_bal <- trainControl(method = "cv",
                         number = 5,
                         sampling = "down")

model_rf_bal <- train(AtRisk ~ ., 
                      data = train_full,
                      method = "rf",
                      trControl = ctrl_bal,
                      ntree = 100)
plot(varImp(model_rf_bal),
     main = "Variable Importance - Random Forest")

Confirm model exists

print(model_rf_bal)

Modeling Statistics

The baseline logistic regression model achieved a high overall accuracy of 98.69%. However, this result was misleading due to the strong class imbalance in the dataset. The model performed poorly in identifying at-risk students, as reflected in a low balanced accuracy of 0.64 and a low recall for the minority class. In practice, the model primarily predicted that students were not at risk, resulting in a large number of missed cases.

After applying resampling techniques, the performance of the logistic regression model improved substantially. The balanced model achieved an accuracy of 91.33% and a balanced accuracy of 0.93. More importantly, the number of correctly identified at-risk students increased from 1,320 to 4,267. This demonstrates that resampling can significantly improve model performance in imbalanced datasets by prioritizing the detection of the minority class.

The decision tree model produced results similar to the baseline logistic regression model. Although it achieved a high accuracy of 98.58%, it exhibited poor performance in identifying at-risk students, with a balanced accuracy of 57%. This indicates that the decision tree was also heavily influenced by the majority class and was not effective for the primary objective of the study.

The random forest model, when combined with resampling, produced strong results. It achieved an accuracy of 90.24% and a balanced accuracy of approximately 92.5%. The model demonstrated a high recall of approximately 94.8%, indicating that it successfully identified the majority of at-risk students. However, this performance came at the cost of lower precision, as the model generated a relatively large number of false positives.

Discussion

Modeling Interpretations

Variable importance results from the random forest model confirm that psychological variables dominate predictive performance . This indicates that the model is more effective at identifying students who are already experiencing distress rather than detecting early warning signs. Behavioral variables, while weaker predictors individually, may still play an important role in early intervention contexts where psychological data is not yet available.

Key Patterns Found

Overall, the findings suggest a layered structure in the data. Behavioral variables provide early but weak signals of potential risk, while psychological variables offer strong but less independent predictive power. This pattern indicates that mental health risk may develop progressively, beginning with behavioral strain and evolving into measurable psychological distress.This progression aligns with theoretical understandings of mental health development, where prolonged behavioral strain can contribute to increased psychological distress over time.(APA)

Overall Result Interpretations

The results of this study highlight the importance of properly addressing class imbalance in classification problems. While the baseline models achieved high accuracy, they failed to meet the primary objective of identifying at-risk students. This demonstrates that accuracy alone is not an appropriate metric in imbalanced settings and that alternative measures such as recall and balanced accuracy are necessary for meaningful evaluation.

The comparison between models reveals a clear trade off between predictive performance and interpretability. The random forest model achieved the highest recall, making it the most effective at identifying at-risk students. This makes it particularly useful in contexts where missing a vulnerable individual carries significant consequences. However, the model also produced a higher number of false positives, which may limit its practical application. In contrast, the logistic regression model provided a more balanced performance and offered greater interpretability, allowing for clearer understanding of the relationships between predictors and the outcome.

Overall, the random forest model provided the best balance between recall and overall performance. This makes it the most effective model for identifying at-risk students, while logistic regression offered greater interpretability at the cost of slightly lower performance. An important point to consider is how strong predictive performance of psychological variables may overstate the model’s real world usefulness, as these measures are often identified through assessment processes that already indicate elevated risk.

Limitations and Future Work

This study has several limitations. First, the dataset is likely synthetically generated, which may limit the generalizability of the results to real-world populations. Second, the presence of strong class imbalance required the use of resampling techniques, which can introduce additional variability into the modeling process. Third, some of the predictors, particularly stress, anxiety and depression, are closely related to the outcome variable which may inflate predictive performance. Additionally, the cross-sectional nature of the dataset limits the ability to infer causal relationships between predictors and mental health risk. Future research could address these limitations by applying the same methodology to real-world datasets, such as clinical or survey-based data. Additional modeling approaches, including gradient boosting methods could also be explored to further improve predictive performance. Finally, incorporating longitudinal data could provide insight into how mental health risk evolves over time.

Conclusion

The study demonstrates that classification models can be effectively used to identify students at risk of poor mental health. While baseline models were misleading due to class imbalance, the application of resampling techniques significantly improved model performance. Among the models evaluated, the random forest model achieved the highest recall and was most effective at identifying at-risk students, while logistic regression provided a more interpretable and balanced alternative. A key implication of this study is the distinction between predictive accuracy and practical usefulness. While models that include psychological variables achieve high performance, they rely on information that may only be available after a student is already experiencing distress. In contrast, behavioral variables, although less predictive, may offer more practical value for early detection and intervention. Overall, the findings suggest that combining behavioral and psychological factors provides the most effective approach for predicting mental health risk. These results highlight the importance of selecting appropriate evaluation metrics and modeling strategies when working with imbalanced data and offer practical insights for identifying vulnerable student populations.
